newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian cyclone weakens but death toll rises to six.
newsitem.headline: Indian cyclone weakens but death toll rises to six.

text.p: A powerful cyclone that threatened to lash India's southeast coast on Thursday has weakened and moved slightly away but is still dangerous, meteorological officials said.
"It has weakened temporarily and moved slightly away. But the danger persists," said J.V.M. Naidu, head of the cyclone warning centre at Visakhapatnam port in Andhra Pradesh state.
Officials in the state capital of Hyderabad said four more people had died in East Godavari district in house collapses or by falling trees, taking the toll since Wednesday to six.
They said around 335,000 people had been evacuated from 780 villages along a coastal stretch 90 km (56 miles) long and 10 km (six miles) wide ahead of the storm.
Naidu said the storm, which was earlier predicted to hit the state by noon Thursday, could still turn towards the coast and cross land near Machilipatnam port by evening or night.
"It is quite possible that it takes a loop and comes back with further intensification," Naidu told Reuters by telephone.

"The severe cyclonic storm with a core of hurricane winds is now reduced to a severe cyclonic storm," he said. "The difference is there are no hurricane winds now and the wind speed has fallen to 90-120 kph (56-75 miles per hour) now from 150-180 kph (94-113 mph) earlier."
It would be the second in a month to hit Andhra Pradesh. At least 2,000 people were killed or are missing after last month's cyclone.
Naidu said the storm's potential to whip up tidal waves was also reduced.
"We predict tidal waves of one to two metres (three to six feet) high when the storm hits the coast against two to three metres (six to nine feet) forecast earlier," he said.
In November 1977, a severe cyclone whipped up tidal waves killing more than 10,000 people in villages near Machilipatnam.
Naidu said the storm, which lingered around 90 km (56 miles) southeast off Machilipatnam port in the Bay of Bengal for more than 10 hours, had moved 30 km (18 miles) in the same direction.
Relief officials said evacuation of people from vulnerable areas along the coast continued despite reports that the cyclone had lost some strength.
"We are moving people from the coastal villages forcibly, with the help of police," said a senior official. "There's a tendency among people to take warnings lightly and move to safety on their own."
Officials said about 60,000 people were evacuated from Krishna district, of which Machilipatnam is the headquarters.
"We know that the storm is weakening. But we don't want to take any chances," said the official.
Moderate to heavy rain, accompanied by winds, had been reported in the coastal areas, meteorological officials said.

"But tidal waves and cyclonic winds have not yet started," said Hyderabad meteorological centre director C.V.V. Bhadram. "It is pretty difficult to predict when the storm will hit the coast. Its erratic behaviour makes it unpredictable."

Port officials in Kakinada said they had moved nine ships out of the harbour to avoid their being buffeted by rough seas. Rail and road services were suspended and power switched off in areas likely to be hit by the cyclone.
Officials said the latest cyclone could cause more damage to property and crops in the agriculturally-rich state than the previous one, which inflicted losses worth 50 billion rupees ($1.4 billion).
They said sugarcane, cotton and tobacco were among the standing crops likely to be affected by the rain and flooding if the storm hits the state.
